Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I want to remember what worked before I plan the next meeting. I arrived at six ten, and the room was already warm because the afternoon class had left the radiator on. Mira was setting out small cards, and Jonas had brought the old desk lamp with the green shade. Our teacher, Elena, started by asking everyone to say one thing that felt easier than last week. I said I could hear the difference between ship and sheep more clearly when I stopped trying to make my mouth move too quickly.

Section 1: The warm-up. We began with a slow breath and a long hum. Then Elena asked us to hold the vowel in sheep for two beats and let the jaw relax. She reminded us that the goal was not to make a perfect sound on the first try, but to notice where the tongue rested. Mira said, “I can hear the difference now, but I lose it when I read a whole sentence.” Elena answered that this was normal and that short practice could help us carry the sound into ordinary speech. Nobody had to perform for the group, and people could pass when it was their turn. That made the room feel less like an exam and more like a workshop.

We wrote three pairs on the board: ship, sheep; full, fool; and live, leave. Elena said that the spelling could be a clue, but it was not a reliable map, and we should listen to the sound inside each word rather than guess from the letters. First, we stretched the longer vowel in sheep and leave. Then we kept the vowel shorter in ship and live. Jonas asked whether his lips should spread on sheep. Elena said a small smile might help, but he should not force it. She showed us the mouth shape in a hand mirror and pointed out that the tongue stayed forward. I tried the pairs slowly and then at a normal pace. I still mixed up full and fool when I rushed, but I caught the error myself twice.

1. Listen before speaking.
2. Make one change at a time.
3. Do not correct a partner while they are still finishing the sentence.

These were the three reminders Elena put beside the board. She said we could offer a model after asking first, and that a learner might be concentrating on a different sound. I liked that rule because last month I interrupted someone while they were telling a story and then forgot the story entirely. The cards on the table had words from our own conversations, so we practiced with “Leave the key by the window” and “I live near the river.” Those sentences sounded less like a textbook and gave us a reason to care about the contrast.

After the break, we worked on the th sound in three and tree. This part was harder for me because I could feel my tongue wanting to pull back. Elena placed a paper strip in front of my mouth and asked me to watch whether it moved a little when I said three. She said the air should pass without turning the first sound into a t. Mira laughed when the strip flew off the table and then asked if she could try with her hand instead of the paper. Elena said yes and reminded us that there was no single tool everyone had to use. I booked the Tuesday room for our extra practice because the caretaker had changed the schedule, and Tuesday was the only evening the smaller room was free.

We made a short recording on our phones and listened once without judging ourselves. Then we listened again for the first sound in three and tree. I noticed that on the first take I had said tree both times. On the second take, I slowed down and got three clearly, but the rest of the sentence sounded stiff. Elena suggested that I record a sentence I actually use at work instead of repeating the word by itself, so I tried, “There are three folders on the desk.” The recording sounded more natural, and I could hear the difference when I listened with my eyes closed. She cautioned us not to treat one good recording as proof that the habit was settled and said we would need to check again next week.

Before we left, we planned a ten-minute practice for home, not a long list that would become another chore. I will listen to the audio from class once each morning and choose two sentences from my notebook to say aloud. Mira will practice the sheep and ship pairs while she walks to the bus stop. Jonas wants to ask his sister to read a paragraph with him, but he will ask whether she has time first. Elena told us to write down one question rather than search for every answer online. I wrote down, “When does a clear sound become an unnatural one?” because I sometimes exaggerate the vowel when I am nervous.

Well, the best part of the lesson was that nobody pretended pronunciation was only about copying a native speaker. Elena said the aim was to make our meaning easier to follow while keeping our own voices. She gave the example of a customer who had understood her perfectly even though she had paused over a word, and she said a pause was not a failure. I want to remember that when I lead the reading group next month. I thanked her and helped stack the cards. Mira took the green lamp back to her car, and Jonas checked that the radiator was off.
